dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Fabrikam plans to run a stateless web tier on a Virtual Machine Scale Set that uses Flexible orchestration. The instances will be deployed from an image version stored in an Azure Compute Gallery. What is the maximum number of VM instances that the scale set can contain?
spiegazione: Correct: 1,000. Microsoft Learn states that you can add up to 1,000 VMs to a scale set in Flexible orchestration mode, and the comparison table lists a maximum instance count (with fault domain guarantees) of 1,000 for Flexible orchestration. Scale sets support up to 1,000 instances for standard marketplace images and for custom images published through the Azure Compute Gallery. Why the others are wrong: 100 is the maximum instance count with fault domain guarantees for Uniform orchestration, and is also the range limit (0-100 VMs) when a Uniform scale set uses a single placement group (singlePlacementGroup = true) - it is not the Flexible limit. 200 is the maximum number of VMs in an availability set, a different availability construct, and is also the Flexible limit only in the narrow case of VM sizes that do not support memory preserving updates combined with fixed spreading. 600 is the instance limit that applies when a scale set is created from a managed image rather than a marketplace or Azure Compute Gallery image, so it does not apply to this Compute Gallery deployment.
tags: vmss,flexible orchestration,scale set limits,instance count,azure compute gallery

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: An engineer creates a Virtual Machine Scale Set by using an Azure Resource Manager template that does not include an upgradePolicy property. Several weeks later, the template is edited to reference a newer image version and is redeployed to the same scale set. What happens to the VM instances that already exist in the scale set?
opzione_a: All existing instances are brought down at the same time and upgraded to the new image immediately.
opzione_b: Existing instances are upgraded in batches of 20 percent, with a health check between each batch.
opzione_c: Existing instances are not changed until you manually upgrade them; only instances added afterwards use the new model.
opzione_d: The redeployment fails because the upgradePolicy property is required when the image reference changes.
spiegazione: Correct: existing instances are unchanged until manually upgraded. Microsoft Learn states that if you do not explicitly set the upgrade policy mode, it defaults to manual. With a manual upgrade policy mode, nothing happens automatically to the existing virtual machines when changes occur to the scale set model, and new instances added to the scale set use the most up-to-date model available. The administrator must explicitly trigger an upgrade on the existing instances. Why the others are wrong: bringing all instances down at once describes the automatic upgrade policy mode, where the scale set makes no guarantees about the order of virtual machines being brought down and might take down all VMs at the same time; that is not the default. Upgrading in batches describes the rolling upgrade policy mode, which must be explicitly selected and additionally requires application health monitoring; 20 percent is the default maxBatchInstancePercent of the rolling upgrade policy, but rolling mode is not the default mode. The deployment does not fail: upgradePolicy is optional, and omitting it simply yields the manual default.
tags: vmss,upgrade policy,manual upgrade,scale set model,arm template

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A scale set named vmss-app was created in Uniform orchestration mode six months ago. The operations team now requires that the individual instances be protected by Azure Backup, which Uniform orchestration does not support. You must meet the requirement with the supported approach. What should you do?
opzione_a: Run az vmss update and set the orchestration mode of vmss-app to Flexible.
opzione_b: Create a new scale set that uses Flexible orchestration mode and redeploy the workload to it.
opzione_c: Set the singlePlacementGroup property of vmss-app to false and register the instances with a Recovery Services vault.
opzione_d: Increase the platformFaultDomainCount of vmss-app to 5 and enable the Azure Backup extension on each instance.
spiegazione: Correct: recreate the scale set in Flexible orchestration mode. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that the orchestration mode is defined when you create the scale set and cannot be changed or updated later. Because the Azure Backup comparison table shows Azure Backup as supported for Flexible orchestration and not supported for Uniform orchestration, the only way to meet the requirement is to deploy a new scale set in Flexible mode and move the workload. Why the others are wrong: az vmss update cannot change the orchestration mode; the mode is immutable after creation, so this command cannot satisfy the requirement. Changing singlePlacementGroup only controls whether a Uniform scale set spans one or multiple placement groups (affecting the 0-100 versus 0-1,000 instance range); it has no bearing on Azure Backup support, which is blocked because Uniform instances are scale-set-specific VMs rather than standard IaaS VMs. Changing platformFaultDomainCount only controls fault domain spreading and likewise does not make Uniform instances compatible with Azure Backup; there is no Azure Backup extension that works around this limitation.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Northwind runs a production API on a Virtual Machine Scale Set that uses Flexible orchestration. You configure a rolling upgrade policy so that model changes roll out in batches. Which additional component must you configure so that the scale set can monitor application health during the rolling upgrade?
opzione_a: An Azure Load Balancer health probe attached to the backend pool.
opzione_b: The Application Health extension on the scale set instances.
opzione_c: An Azure Monitor Agent deployment with a data collection rule that collects performance counters.
opzione_d: An availability test in Application Insights that targets the API endpoint.
spiegazione: Correct: the Application Health extension. Microsoft Learn states that when using a rolling upgrade policy on Virtual Machine Scale Sets with Flexible orchestration, the scale set must also use the Application Health extension to monitor application health. Rolling upgrades depend on per-instance health signals to decide whether a batch succeeded and whether to continue, pause, or stop the upgrade. Why the others are wrong: a load balancer health probe is a valid health source only for Uniform orchestration, where Learn says the scale set must have a health probe or use the Application Health extension. For Flexible orchestration, application health via a Standard Load Balancer health probe is explicitly listed as an unsupported parameter, and the guidance is to use the Application Health extension on instances instead. The Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule gathers telemetry into a Log Analytics workspace for monitoring and alerting, but it does not report instance health to the scale set orchestrator and cannot gate a rolling upgrade. An Application Insights availability test monitors endpoint reachability from outside Azure and produces alerts, but it likewise provides no per-instance health signal to the scale set.
tags: vmss,rolling upgrade,application health extension,flexible orchestration,upgrade policy

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: An autoscale setting that targets a Virtual Machine Scale Set contains three profiles: a fixed-date profile that covers a product launch on 20 November, a recurrence profile that covers weekday business hours, and a default profile. On Friday 20 November at 10:00 local time, all three profiles are applicable. Which profile does the autoscale engine execute?
opzione_a: The default profile, because it always acts as the fallback and overrides scheduled profiles.
opzione_b: The recurrence profile, because weekday business hours are more specific than a single date.
opzione_c: The fixed-date profile, because fixed-date profiles are evaluated first and the first suitable profile is used.
opzione_d: All three profiles, because autoscale merges the rules and uses the highest maximum capacity.
spiegazione: Correct: the fixed-date profile. Microsoft Learn states that each time the autoscale service runs, profiles are evaluated in the order fixed-date profiles, then recurring profiles, then the default profile, and the first suitable profile that is found is used. Because 20 November at 10:00 falls inside the fixed-date window, that profile matches first and is the one executed. Why the others are wrong: the default profile runs only when no other applicable profile exists for the current date and time; it is last in the evaluation order, not an override. The recurrence profile is second in the evaluation order and is only selected when no fixed-date profile applies; the engine does not rank profiles by how specific they appear. Autoscale does not merge profiles: Learn states that each time the autoscale engine runs, it executes one profile, so capacity limits and rules are never combined across profiles.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A single autoscale profile that targets a Virtual Machine Scale Set contains two scale-in rules. The first triggers when the average Percentage CPU is less than 30 percent. The second triggers when the average Network In is less than 500,000 bytes. During the evaluation window the average Percentage CPU is 22 percent, but Network In remains far above its threshold. No scale-out rule is triggered, and the current instance count is above the profile minimum. What does autoscale do?
opzione_a: It scales in, because at least one scale-in rule was triggered.
opzione_b: It does not scale in, because autoscale scales in only when all of the scale-in rules in the profile are triggered.
opzione_c: It scales in, but only by the smaller of the two instance counts calculated by the rules.
opzione_d: It scales out to the profile default instance count, because the rule set is in conflict.
spiegazione: Correct: no scale-in occurs. Microsoft Learn states that autoscale scales out if any scale-out rule is met, but scales in only when all scale-in rules are met. Because the Network In scale-in rule is not triggered, the AND condition across scale-in rules fails and the instance count is left unchanged. This asymmetry is deliberate and biased toward availability. Why the others are wrong: the any-rule-is-enough behaviour applies to scale-out rules (direction Increase), not to scale-in rules, so a single triggered scale-in rule is insufficient. Choosing the smaller calculated count describes nothing in the documented algorithm; in fact, when all scale-in rules do trigger, Learn states autoscale scales in by as little as possible, resulting in the highest of the calculated instance counts, not the smallest. Autoscale does not scale out to the default instance count here: the default capacity is used only when there is a problem reading the resource metric, and metrics are being read successfully in this scenario.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A zone-spanning Virtual Machine Scale Set is deployed across three availability zones and has the OldestVM scale-in policy configured. The instances are currently distributed as follows. Zone 1 contains instance IDs 3, 4, 5 and 10. Zone 2 contains instance IDs 2, 6, 9 and 11. Zone 3 contains instance IDs 1, 7 and 8. Lower instance IDs correspond to older virtual machines, and no instance is protected. Autoscale triggers a scale-in of one instance. Which instance does the scale set delete?
opzione_a: Instance 1, because it is the oldest virtual machine in the entire scale set.
opzione_b: Instance 2, because it is the oldest virtual machine in the zones that are over-provisioned.
opzione_c: Instance 3, because it is the oldest virtual machine in Zone 1.
opzione_d: Instance 11, because it has the highest instance ID in the scale set.
spiegazione: Correct: instance 2. Microsoft Learn documents that the OldestVM policy deletes the oldest created VM after first balancing VMs across availability zones for zone-spanning scale sets. Zone 1 and Zone 2 each hold four instances while Zone 3 holds three, so the scale set is unbalanced and the deletion candidate must come from Zone 1 or Zone 2. Across those two zones the oldest VM is instance 2 in Zone 2, so instance 2 is deleted. This matches the worked example in the Learn documentation. Why the others are wrong: instance 1 is indeed the oldest VM in the scale set, but it sits in Zone 3, which already has the fewest instances; deleting it would worsen the zone imbalance, and zone balancing takes precedence over the scale-in policy. Instance 3 is the oldest VM in Zone 1 and is a valid zone candidate, but instance 2 is older than instance 3, so the OldestVM policy selects instance 2 from among the two eligible zones. Instance 11 is the newest VM; deleting it would be the behaviour of the NewestVM scale-in policy, not OldestVM, and the highest instance ID rule belongs to the Default policy.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Contoso must choose an orchestration mode for a new Virtual Machine Scale Set. Which capabilities are supported by Flexible orchestration but NOT supported by Uniform orchestration? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Protecting the scale set instances by using Azure Backup.
opzione_b: Adding an existing standalone Azure virtual machine to the scale set.
opzione_c: Running Spot priority instances and Regular priority instances in the same scale set.
opzione_d: Performing image-based automatic OS image upgrades on the instances.
opzione_e: Scaling the instance count automatically based on host metric thresholds.
spiegazione: Correct answers a, b and c. Azure Backup: the Learn comparison table lists Azure Backup as supported for Flexible orchestration and not supported for Uniform orchestration, because Uniform instances are scale-set-specific VMs (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets/virtualMachines) that are not compatible with Azure Backup or Azure Site Recovery, whereas Flexible instances are standard IaaS VMs. Adding an existing VM: the table row 'Add/remove existing VM to the group' is Yes for Flexible and No for Uniform, since Uniform can only manage VMs implicitly created from its configuration model. Mixing Spot and Regular: Learn states that Flexible supports both Spot and Regular priority instances in the same scale set, while for Uniform 'instances must either be all Spot or all Regular'. Why the others are wrong: automatic OS image upgrades are the reverse of the requirement - Learn lists Automatic OS Updates as Yes for Uniform and No for Flexible, and image-based automatic OS upgrades appear in the list of parameters not supported with Flexible orchestration. Metrics-based autoscale is supported by both modes: the Learn table shows automatic scaling (manual, metrics based, schedule based) as Yes for Flexible and Yes for Uniform, so it does not differentiate them.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: You are hardening the rolling upgrade policy of a Virtual Machine Scale Set that hosts a production API across three availability zones. The Application Health extension is already reporting health. Which configuration actions correctly achieve their stated goal? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Set maxBatchInstancePercent to 10 so that no more than 10 percent of the instances are upgraded in a single batch.
opzione_b: Set maxUnhealthyInstancePercent to 20 so that the rolling upgrade stops if more than 20 percent of the instances in the scale set report as unhealthy.
opzione_c: Enable MaxSurge so that new instances that use the latest model are created and marked healthy before instances that use the old model are deleted.
opzione_d: Enable cross-zone upgrade so that the rolling upgrade guarantees that only one availability zone is upgraded at a time.
opzione_e: Set pauseTimeBetweenBatches to PT0S so that the scale set verifies that every instance in a batch is healthy before starting the next batch.
spiegazione: Correct answers a, b and c. maxBatchInstancePercent specifies how many of the total instances you want upgraded at one time; Learn's example states that a batch size of 20 percent with 10 instances produces batches of two instances, so setting it to 10 correctly caps each batch at 10 percent. maxUnhealthyInstancePercent specifies the total number of instances allowed to be marked unhealthy before and during the rolling upgrade; Learn's example states that with a value of 20 and a scale set of 10 instances, the rolling upgrade stops if more than two instances report unhealthy. MaxSurge is documented as creating new instances in batches using the latest scale model and, once the batch is successfully created and marked healthy, deleting instances in batches matching the old model, which improves service uptime during upgrades. Why the others are wrong: enable cross-zone upgrade does the opposite of the stated goal. Learn states it allows the scale set to ignore availability zone boundaries when determining batches, essentially treating a zone-spanning deployment as a regional (nonzonal) one; it does not confine an upgrade to one zone at a time. Setting pauseTimeBetweenBatches to PT0S does not verify health at all - the setting only specifies how long the scale set waits between finishing one batch and starting the next, and PT0S means no wait. Batch health gating is governed by maxUnhealthyInstancePercent and maxUnhealthyUpgradedInstancePercent instead.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: You are authoring an autoscale rule for a Virtual Machine Scale Set in an Azure Resource Manager template. The rule must meet the following requirements. The Percentage CPU metric must be sampled and averaged once every minute. Each time autoscale runs, it must evaluate the metrics collected over the preceding 10 minutes. When the threshold is exceeded, the scale set must add instances. After a scale action completes, no further scale action may occur for 10 minutes. Select the appropriate value for each setting.
spiegazione: timeGrain = PT1M. Learn defines timeGrain as the metric sampling duration, and states that timeGrain = 'PT1M' means the metrics are aggregated every 1 minute by using the aggregation method specified in the statistic element, which matches the requirement to sample and average once per minute. PT10M and PT30M would sample every 10 or 30 minutes and do not meet the requirement. timeWindow = PT10M. Learn defines timeWindow as the amount of time to look back for metrics, and states that timeWindow = 'PT10M' means that every time autoscale runs, it queries metrics for the past 10 minutes. PT1M would look back only one minute and would react to transient spikes; PT1H would look back an hour. direction = Increase. Learn states that the scaleAction direction is 'Increase' to scale out, or 'Decrease' to scale in; adding instances therefore requires Increase. Decrease would remove instances and None is not a valid documented direction value. cooldown = PT10M. Learn defines cooldown as the amount of time to wait after a scale operation before scaling again, giving the example that cooldown = 'PT10M' means autoscale does not attempt to scale again for another 10 minutes. PT2M and PT5M would permit another scale action after only 2 or 5 minutes, which violates the requirement.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: You are designing a Virtual Machine Scale Set for a quorum-based service in a region that supports availability zones. The design must meet the following requirements. Instances must be spread across zones 1, 2 and 3. Within each zone, Azure must spread the instances across as many fault domains as possible. Any scaling operation that would leave the zones unevenly populated must be blocked, even when a zone is unavailable. When autoscale scales in, the scale set must remove the most recently created virtual machine from an over-provisioned zone. Select the appropriate value for each setting.
opzione_a: Availability zone configuration: [Regional (nonzonal) | Zonal (single zone) | Zone spanning]
spiegazione: Availability zone configuration = Zone spanning. Learn states that a zone spanning scale set spreads instances across all selected zones ('zones': ['1','2','3']) and is the recommended model, meeting the 99.99 percent SLA. Zonal places all instances in a single zone and regional (nonzonal) provides no guarantee of balance or spread across zones, so neither satisfies the requirement. platformFaultDomainCount = 1. Learn states that max spreading is platformFaultDomainCount = 1, and that with max spreading the scale set spreads your VMs across as many fault domains as possible within each zone; Microsoft recommends max spreading for most workloads. 5 is fixed spreading across exactly five fault domains, and fixed spreading with 2 or 3 fault domains is supported for regional (nonzonal) deployments only and is invalid for zone-spanning scale sets, which must use 1 or 5. zoneBalance = true. Learn states you can specify strict zone balance by setting 'zoneBalance': 'true', and that with strict zone balancing the scale set must be balanced at all times and any scaling operation that would result in an unbalanced scale set is blocked, even if one or more zones are down. false selects the default best-effort mode, which deliberately permits a temporary imbalance when a single zone is unavailable and therefore does not meet the requirement. scaleInPolicy rules = NewestVM. Learn states the NewestVM policy deletes the newest, or most recently created, virtual machine in the scale set after balancing VMs across availability zones. Default balances across zones and fault domains and then deletes the VM with the highest instance ID, while OldestVM deletes the oldest VM; neither targets the most recently created VM by creation time.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda:
A Virtual Machine Scale Set named vmss-batch uses autoscale and has the OldestVM scale-in policy configured on the scale set model. The oldest instance in the scale set is running a long batch job that must not be interrupted, so you set the protectFromScaleIn property to true on that instance and leave protectFromScaleSetActions unset. You need to evaluate the resulting behaviour. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. When autoscale triggers a scale-in, the protected instance is skipped even though it is the oldest virtual machine in the scale set.
2. An administrator can still delete the protected instance manually at any time.
3. Setting protectFromScaleIn also prevents the instance from being upgraded when the scale set model changes.
opzione_a: When autoscale triggers a scale-in, the protected instance is skipped even though it is the oldest virtual machine in the scale set.
opzione_b: An administrator can still delete the protected instance manually at any time.
opzione_c: Setting protectFromScaleIn also prevents the instance from being upgraded when the scale set model changes.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Learn states that a protected virtual machine is not deleted through a scale-in action regardless of the scale-in policy applied, and gives exactly this example: if VM_0 (the oldest VM in the scale set) is protected from scale-in and the scale set has the OldestVM policy enabled, VM_0 is not considered for being scaled in even though it is the oldest VM. Statement 2 is Yes. Learn states that for protect from scale-in, user-initiated instance operations, including instance delete, are not blocked, and that a protected virtual machine can be manually deleted by the user at any time regardless of the scale-in policy enabled on the scale set. Instance protection guards against autoscale-initiated scale-in, not against deliberate administrator action. Statement 3 is No. Learn states that protectFromScaleIn protects the instance only from autoscale-initiated scale-in, and that operations initiated on the scale set (upgrade, reimage, deallocate, and so on) are not blocked. Blocking scale set operations such as upgrade requires the separate protectFromScaleSetActions property, which was left unset here. Note that protectFromScaleSetActions also implies protection from autoscale-initiated scale-in, and you cannot specify protectFromScaleIn as false while setting protectFromScaleSetActions to true.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda:
A zone-spanning Virtual Machine Scale Set is deployed across availability zones 1, 2 and 3 and uses the default zone balance mode. Following a recent incident, zone 1 contains 1 VM, zone 2 contains 3 VMs, and zone 3 contains 3 VMs. All instances were created successfully and are running. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. The scale set is currently considered unbalanced.
2. If zone 2 and zone 3 both become unavailable, the scale set can still scale out by adding instances to zone 1.
3. Adding another availability zone to the scale set automatically redistributes the existing VM instances into the new zone.
opzione_a: The scale set is currently considered unbalanced.
opzione_b: If zone 2 and zone 3 both become unavailable, the scale set can still scale out by adding instances to zone 1.
opzione_c: Adding another availability zone to the scale set automatically redistributes the existing VM instances into the new zone.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Learn states that a scale set is considered balanced if each zone has the same number of VMs plus or minus 1 VM. Here zone 1 has 2 fewer VMs than zones 2 and 3, which exceeds the allowed threshold of plus or minus 1 VM. This is the exact scenario in Learn's Example 3 (1 VM in zone 1, 3 VMs in zone 2, 3 VMs in zone 3), which the documentation labels unbalanced. Statement 2 is No. With best-effort zone balancing, which is the default mode, Learn states that if one zone is unavailable the scale set attempts to scale out into the zones that are still available and allows a temporary imbalance, but that this imbalance is only permitted when a single zone is unavailable. It further states that if two or more zones are unavailable, the scale set cannot proceed with scaling operations and any scaling operations are blocked. Because two zones are down, scale-out is blocked. Statement 3 is No. Learn states that when you add availability zones to an existing scale set, existing VMs remain unchanged and do not get moved or redistributed, and that adding a zone does not trigger a rebalancing operation. Zone balancing only happens during scale-out operations when new instances are added, and zone balance does not replace existing instances; rebalancing must be performed manually by scaling out and then scaling in.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: A regional (nonzonal) Virtual Machine Scale Set named vmss-web contains 5 instances in a region that supports availability zones. You must convert vmss-web into a zone-spanning scale set that ends with 5 instances spread across zones 1, 2 and 3, while keeping the workload available throughout. Which four actions should you perform in sequence? Move the appropriate actions from the list to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
opzione_a: Reduce the capacity of the scale set to 5 so that Azure removes the original nonzonal instances.
opzione_b: Verify that platformFaultDomainCount is set to 1 or 5 and that the VM size and disk types are available in all three zones.
opzione_c: Update the zones parameter on the scale set to ["1","2","3"].
opzione_d: Increase the capacity of the scale set to 10 so that 5 new zonal instances are created.
opzione_e: Change the orchestration mode of the scale set from Uniform to Flexible.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, c, d, a. Learn documents that expanding to a zone-spanning scale set is done in three steps - prepare for zone expansion, update the zones parameter on the scale set, then add new zonal instances and remove original instances - and the manual balancing procedure expands the last step into a scale out followed by a scale in. Step b (prepare) comes first because Learn requires validating that the configuration is valid for zonal and zone-spanning scale sets: platformFaultDomainCount must be set to 1 or 5, since fixed spreading with 2 or 3 fault domains is not supported for zonal and zone-spanning scale sets, and you must check quota and that the VM size and disk types are available in the desired zones. Step c updates the zones parameter, which is supported with API version 2023-03-01 or greater. Step d scales out: Learn's worked example for a nonzonal scale set with 5 instances states you should set the capacity to 10 (5 + 5) so the new instances are created across the zones while old instances remain where they are. Step a scales in to 5, and Learn states the platform always prefers removing the nonzonal instances first, then follows the scale set's scale-in policy, leaving 5 zonal instances spread across the zones. Why option e is not used: it is a distractor. Learn states that the orchestration mode is defined when you create the scale set and cannot be changed or updated later, so this action is impossible and is not required for zone expansion in either orchestration mode.
